clips.title: Detecting Breaking API Changes: Better API Management Through Automation
clips.why: Erik Wilde, who has worked on API standards for years, defines what makes an API change breaking from the client's side.
look: A change is judged by what it does to existing clients, not by how big it looks in the diff.
Which kinds of changes break clients, and which usually do not.
Who decides whether a change is breaking: the clients that already exist.
clips.after: fcp's published SDK and the scripts customers write with it are exactly those clients, which is why the rename in the story counts as breaking.

clips.title: Detecting gRPC Schema Breaking Changes with Buf & Local Dev Setup
clips.why: A short demo of buf breaking: change a proto, compare it with the previous version, and read the error.
look: buf compares the current protos with an older version that you point it at.
How the error names the message, the field and what changed.
Think about where this command belongs in a team: in CI, so it can stop a change before it merges.
clips.after: fcp's cloud-client protos get the same check, compared with the merge base on main.

clips.title: Every engineer should know this.. (Expand-Contract Pattern)
clips.why: The expand and contract pattern explained with a database column, the safe way to change any contract that someone else still reads.
look: Why changing a column in one step breaks the code that is still running.
The expand step: add the new column next to the old one.
Notice that nothing is removed in this part: the expand step never breaks a reader.
clips.after: The same two steps make the rename in the story safe in the serializer, in the proto and in the database.

practice.q: Which of these API changes is not breaking for an old client?

options.text: Adding a new optional field to a response
options.why: Old clients ignore fields they do not know. That is the expand step of expand and contract.

options.text: Making an optional query parameter required
options.why: Old clients do not send it, so their requests start failing.
For a client, a rename removes the field it reads.

practice.q: Print the commit where your branch left main.
practice.hint: Two words joined by a hyphen.
practice.why: git merge-base prints the last common commit, the right "before" for every breaking-change check.

practice.q: Make oasdiff exit with an error code when it finds an error-level change, so the CI job fails.
practice.hint: The short name of the error level.
practice.why: Without --fail-on, oasdiff only prints. With --fail-on ERR it exits with 1 on any error-level change.

practice.q: Put the steps of the merge-base check in order.
items: Find the merge base with git merge-base HEAD main
Check it out into a second folder with git worktree add
Generate base.yaml from that folder and head.yaml from the branch
Run oasdiff breaking on the two files with --fail-on ERR
If it fails, change the API in an expand step instead of silencing the check
practice.why: The check needs the old contract from the old code, the new contract from the new code, and a comparison. The fix is a safer change, never a quieter check.

practice.q: In a proto message, field 3 workgroup is no longer needed. What is the safe change?

options.text: Delete it and give number 3 to the next new field.
options.why: Old clients still send number 3 with the old meaning, and the new code would read it as something else.

options.text: Rename it, because the number stays the same on the wire.
options.why: The number survives, but the generated code changes name, and buf's PACKAGE rules report it.

options.text: Keep it with [deprecated = true], and give any new field a new number.
options.why: Old clients keep working, readers are warned, and no number is ever reused.
